there-was-a-father-1942.gazette: Ozu released this in 1942, with Japan five years into war in China and a year into the Pacific, and every script passing a government reader before a camera turned. Onscreen there is no war: a widowed schoolteacher resigns after a student drowns on a school outing, takes work in Tokyo, and sees his son a few days a year. The version that survives is a shortened postwar print — some of what one regime's censors approved, the next regime's censors cut.

the-best-years-of-our-lives-1946.gazette: Harold Russell was not an actor. He had lost both hands in a stateside training accident and was appearing in an Army rehabilitation short when Wyler cast him as Homer — hooks, and no double. The picture opened in 1946 with the country still absorbing its returning armies, and it put the paperwork of readjustment onscreen: prosthetics, bank loans, marriages that had aged three years in absence.

late-spring-1949.gazette: Japan in 1949 was still an occupied country, and Ozu made a film in which the only crisis is a marriage. Noriko is twenty-seven, keeping house in Kamakura for her widowed father, and the family's real business is arranging a match before the age passes. The camera sits at floor height and does not move; the pressure of the period arrives entirely through who pours whose tea and who is told which lie.
late-spring-1949.prism: The realism contract cuts both ways here. Filming the arrangement as routine makes it look like weather instead of a decision someone made — and the daughter's wedding smile and the father alone with an apple afterward are the same event, shot from the side that didn't have to choose.

stray-dog-1949.gazette: Much of the market footage is the real thing: Ishiro Honda carried a camera into Ueno's black market in 1949 and filmed the stalls and crowds a stolen pistol sends the young detective through. The sequence runs for minutes with almost no dialogue, close and sweating in the summer heat. What survives in it is a documentary record of an economy that officially did not exist.

the-third-man-1949.gazette: Greene and Reed worked from what was in front of them — a Vienna divided among four occupying armies, its inner district patrolled by jeeps carrying one soldier from each. The rubble in frame is the actual rubble, the sewers are the actual sewers, and the racket at the center, penicillin stolen from military hospitals and diluted for resale, was a documented postwar trade. The film's most famous line was improvised on the day; the city underneath it was not.

casque-d-or-1952.gazette: Amélie Élie was a real woman, and in 1902 two Paris gang leaders went to war over her in the streets around Belleville. The press named her Casque d'Or for her hair and ran the feud as front-page copy for months. Becker keeps the affair and alters its ending: the historical Manda went not to the guillotine but to the penal colony in French Guiana, and died there.
casque-d-or-1952.prism: Trading the bagne for the blade reads as severity and works as mercy. A guillotine is one bad morning; Guiana was decades of them, and the version audiences remember is the shorter sentence.

tokyo-story-1953.gazette: An elderly couple leaves Onomichi for Tokyo in 1953 and finds their children too busy to receive them — the doctor's practice runs to schedule, the beauty parlor has customers waiting. The one with time is Noriko, a daughter-in-law widowed by the war eight years earlier. Ozu films the whole displacement at eye level from a seated position, and a generation's migration to the cities registers as a shortage of afternoons.

senso-1954.gazette: It begins in the Fenice during Il Trovatore, green-white-red leaflets dropping from the upper tiers onto an audience of Austrian officers: Venice in 1866, in the last months of foreign rule. Visconti rebuilt the period down to the buttons and staged Custoza as it was actually fought — an Italian defeat, not a founding victory. The Risorgimento arrives here as a disordered field, an occupying army's exit, and a countess's private accounting.

seven-samurai-1954.gazette: Kurosawa built the village whole on the Izu peninsula and then spent close to a year inside it, past budget and past schedule, with Toho halting production more than once. The final battle was shot in winter rain with mud to the ankles, the water dosed with ink so it would read on film. What comes out is the sixteenth century as labor: rice counted out as wages, armor scavenged off corpses, farmers who are neither noble nor innocent.
seven-samurai-1954.prism: The famous mud is a production fact before it is a historical one — the misery onscreen belongs to the crew as much as to the era. That's the trade: an authenticity that registers in the body, bought with a shoot that nearly failed to finish.

tokyo-twilight-1957.gazette: The coldest of Ozu's family pictures runs through a Tokyo winter of mahjong parlors, late trains, and a clinic a young woman visits alone; abortion had been legal in Japan since 1948 and was common enough by the fifties to pass without comment. The household at the center has a mother who left years ago and two daughters who were never told the whole of it. Nothing rises above a conversational register, and the film ends with a mother watching an empty platform as her train pulls out.

equinox-flower-1958.gazette: Ozu shot his first color film here, choosing Agfa stock for the way it held red, and the frames fill with kettles and cushions in that register. The plot is a small piece of social history: a company man endorses love matches in public and refuses one at his own table, in the years when Japanese couples were quietly moving from arranged marriages to their own choosing. He is maneuvered into consent by the women of the house, and the surrender is filmed as a train ride.

hiroshima-mon-amour-1959.gazette: Resnais was commissioned to make a documentary about the bomb and delivered this instead, keeping the footage — museum vitrines, newsreel, hospital wards, hair. The other history in it belongs to Nevers in 1944, where French women who had taken German lovers were shorn in public and walked through the streets by their neighbors. The film sets the two side by side and declines to rank them.
hiroshima-mon-amour-1959.prism: Setting a provincial haircut beside an erased city is the whole risk, and the film never claims the scales match. The claim is narrower and colder: both were survived, both were tidied away on schedule, and the tidying is the thing actually being filmed.

pickpocket-1959.gazette: Bresson brought in Kassagi, a professional sleight-of-hand artist, to choreograph the thefts, then cast him in the film as one of the accomplices. The hands carry the performance: wallets lifted at the Gare de Lyon in a relay, a watch off a wrist, a jacket held open a half-second too long. Nothing is hidden in a cutaway, and the technique is legible enough that the film has been called, not entirely as a joke, a manual.

vagabond-1985.gazette: Varda shot in the Languedoc in winter and filled the frame with people who lived there — vine-pruners, a garage mechanic, a goatherd with a philosophy degree — many of them non-professionals speaking close to their own lives. The film opens with Mona dead in a ditch and reconstructs her backward out of what strangers remember, which is mostly what she cost them. The camera keeps sliding leftward across the landscape and letting her walk out of the frame.

dust-in-the-wind-1986.gazette: The script came out of Wu Nien-jen's own youth in the coal country above Keelung, and Hou filmed it where it happened: the mine mouths, the single-track railway, the town whose only future was in Taipei. A boy and a girl go down to the city for printing and tailoring work, and the film holds still while the years take them. He is sent off to military service; she marries the postman who had been delivering his letters.
dust-in-the-wind-1986.prism: The long takes aren't patience for its own sake — they're the exchange rate. Nothing dramatic takes the girl away, only the ordinary arithmetic of a country moving off the mountain, and the camera stays wide enough to show that nobody decided it.
